methods.label: Check the hypothesis and a counterexample
methods.explanation: The stated criterion requires two intersecting lines, so it cannot be applied directly to two parallel lines. For example, let planes \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) intersect along a line \(r\). In \(\alpha\), choose two distinct lines \(l\) and \(m\), each parallel to \(r\) and different from \(r\). Neither line meets \(\beta\): any common point would have to lie on \(r\), which neither line meets. Thus both lines are parallel to \(\beta\), although the planes intersect. Thus the replacement does not guarantee parallel planes, and C is correct.
methods.levelReason: The construction uses intersecting planes, planar parallel lines, and the definition of line-plane parallelism, all within or below Required mathematics II.

review.mathematicalCheck: If α and β intersect along r, any point shared by β and a line contained in α must lie on r. The constructed lines avoid r, so both are parallel to β. They are mutually parallel because both are parallel to r. Thus intersecting planes satisfy the replacement hypothesis, establishing C.
